entry.title: Other Spec Review: CSS line-clamp
entry.content:
Specification

https://drafts.csswg.org/css-overflow-4/#suppressing-excess

Explainer

https://github.com/Igalia/explainers/blob/main/css/line-clamp/README.md

Links

  • Previous early design review, if any: N/A
  • An introduction to the feature, aimed at unfamiliar audiences: https://github.com/Igalia/explainers/blob/main/css/line-clamp/README.md#introduction
  • A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal:
    • https://github.com/Igalia/explainers/blob/main/css/line-clamp/README.md#motivation
    • https://medium.com/mofed/css-line-clamp-the-good-the-bad-and-the-straight-up-broken-865413f16e5
  • Alternatives considered: https://
  • Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems: https://github.com/Igalia/explainers/blob/main/css/line-clamp/README.md#examples
  • What do the end-users experience with this proposal: https://
  • User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any: N/A
  • Web Platform Tests: https://wpt.fyi/results/css/css-overflow/line-clamp

The specification

  • Follows the Web Platform Design Principles.
  • Includes Security and Privacy Considerations sections based on answers to the Security/Privacy Questionnaire.

Where and by whom is the work is being done?

  • GitHub repo: https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/
  • Primary contacts:
    • Florian Rivoal (@frivoal), Invited Expert, Editor
    • Andreu Botella (@andreubotella), Igalia, Chromium implementer
  • Organization/project driving the specification: Igalia
  • This work is being funded by: Bloomberg
  • Primary standards group developing this feature: CSS Working Group
  • Group intended to standardize this work: CSS Working Group
  • Incubation and standards groups that have discussed the design:
    • https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/www-style/2018May/0041.html
    • w3c/csswg-drafts#7708

Feedback so far

  • Multi-stakeholder feedback:
    • Chromium comments: Implementing, planning to ship
    • Mozilla comments: mozilla/standards-positions#984 (see also w3c/csswg-drafts#14189)
    • WebKit comments: WebKit/standards-positions#316
    • Interop proposals: 2025, 2026, 2027
  • Major unresolved issues with or opposition to this specification:
    • the current version of the editor's draft doesn't yet reflect the latest status of the working group resolutions in terms of how the syntax space is distributed across the longhands; w3c/csswg-drafts#14508 is a PR making these changes
    • w3c/csswg-drafts#14448, arguing that block-ellipsis's behavior of discarding the line's contents when there are no soft wrap opportunities is "clearly a bad result"
  • Status/issue trackers for implementations:
    • Chrome Status: https://chromestatus.com/feature/4885575595458560
    • Mozilla: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1540681
    • WebKit: There isn't a single meta-issue, but there's work being done: https://bugs.webkit.org/buglist.cgi?quicksearch=line-clamp&list_id=13494808

You should also know that...

  • -webkit-line-clamp has been supported in all mainstream browser engines for years, even though it was not specified anywhere. There are cases, however, where the legacy behavior of mainstream engines is interoperable but where this specification changes the behavior. We don't expect breakage in the wild, since browsers aren't interoperable in many other cases, but it is possible that we might find some.

    • In the legacy behavior, content after the clamp point renders normally, except it is usually outside the box of the -webkit-line-clamp container, so that needs overflow: hidden to hide it. In the spec'd behavior, content after the clamp point becomes invisible and is counted as ink overflow, so overflow: hidden is not needed.
    • In the legacy behavior, if the ellipsis wouldn't fit at the end of a line, glyphs and atomic inlines would be removed off the end of the line to make it fit, as with text-overflow: ellipsis. In the spec'd behavior, inline content at the end of the line is displaced until the last soft wrap opportunity such that the ellipsis fits; and if there are none, the entire contents of the line are displaced.
    • In the legacy behavior, floats can overflow the -webkit-line-clamp container, but since overflow: hidden is almost always used, in practice they will be always clipped to the padding box. In the spec'd behavior, float clearance is not taken into account for the container's automatic sizing (meaning that floats can overflow despite the container establishing an independent formatting context), and floats before the clamp point are clipped to the container's content edge.

  • Review on the naming of line-clamp's longhands would be appreciated. For example, there were questions raised on the name of the block-ellipsis property, since its keywords are ellipsis and no-ellipsis (see w3c/csswg-drafts#13670 (comment)). We would also appreciate feedback on the name of the continue property, considering also that there are plans to extend this property to handle channeling overflow (https://drafts.csswg.org/css-overflow-5/#fragmentation).

  • In Chromium, we are planning to ship line-clamp soon. We would only be shipping line-clamp as a longhand, and only ship its longhands at some point in the future. We will also be changing the legacy behavior of -webkit-line-clamp to match line-clamp at the same time.

entry.title: FYI: SVG textPath side attribute
entry.content:
Hi TAG,

This is an FYI about Chromium's planned implementation of the existing SVG2 side attribute on <textPath>.

During the Intent to Ship discussion, Blink API owners recommended notifying the TAG for awareness. We have already sent the Intent to Ship; apologies for the late notification. This issue is intended as an FYI rather than a request for a full design review, but feedback is welcome.

Feature summary

The side attribute controls which side of a path the text is placed on. Setting side="right" effectively reverses the path direction for text layout.

This allows authors to place text on the inside or outside of a shape, such as a circular path, without duplicating or manually reversing the path data.

Specification

  • SVG2 definition:
    https://w3c.github.io/svgwg/svg2-draft/text.html#TextPathElementSideAttribute
  • Related SVG Working Group discussion about the IDL:
    w3c/svgwg#1086

Implementation references

  • Chromium:
    https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40362379
  • Firefox:
    https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2034371
  • WebKit:
    WebKit/WebKit#66616

Chromium shipping plans

We are targeting Chrome 156, subject to the remaining shipping approvals.

  • ChromeStatus:
    https://chromestatus.com/feature/5422782593761280
  • Intent to Ship discussion:
    https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/d/msgid/blink-dev/6aab4606.edf999b6.27416f.0002.GAE%40google.com

Thanks!

  • A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal: https://w3c.github.io/vcalm/#introduction (prior to the conception of the VCALM specification, the verifiable credential data model had no well-defined APIs to exchange credentials between multiple roles in the three-party model and manage the entire lifecycle of the credentials in a manner that encourages competition and prevents vendor lock-in)
  • Alternatives considered: https://w3c.github.io/vcalm/#relationship-to-other-specifications
  • Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems:
    • https://w3c.github.io/vcalm/#exchange-examples

  • What do the end-users experience with this proposal:
    • https://w3c.github.io/vcalm/#introduction
    • https://w3c.github.io/vcalm/#architecture-overview
    • https://w3c.github.io/vcalm/#exchange-examples
    • https://w3c.github.io/vcalm/#initiating-interactions
  • User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any: Feedback and extensive discussion from production deployments (CA DMV, National Association of Convenience Stores, Conexxus standards work, TruAge) and pilot programs (DHS “plugfest” series, Interoperability “plugfest” series co-organized by Jobs for the Future (JFF) and the Verifiable Credentials for Education W3C task force (VC EDU), California Career Passport usability studies, US First Responders, US Vital Records)

  • This work is being funded by: National Association of Convenience Stores, California DMV, Conexxus, Digital Bazaar, Digital Credentials Consortium

entry.title: Question: Architectural issue: local path hijacking and cloud sync lock-in vs user agency
entry.content:
Ask your question.
Architectural issue (not a spec review): user-agency failure in OS/web workspace sync connectors.

Asks for TAG

  1. Treat automatic remapping of well-known local directories as an architecture/user-agency issue where web and workspace connectors participate.
  2. Record a principle: local file operations must not depend on remote quota or connectivity; an empty remote account must not be allowed to overwrite or dehydrate a larger local tree without an explicit, reversible, step-by-step consent that states the direction of sync and the billing consequence.
  3. Recommend a mandatory “hard severance” that restores independent local paths without leftover placeholders.
